This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - **Overall project**: Build "SwapsEngine" — a high-performance extension of QuantLib replacing its two slowest workflows (swap-curve calibration and bulk swap analytics) with a globally-calibrated, AAD-differentiated, vectorized implementation. QuantLib IS a linked dependency (reuse calendars/schedules/instruments; optimize the hot paths). It is also the correctness oracle and speed baseline to beat.
   - **Setup asks**: project setup, CLAUDE.md rules, git local commits + web backup at major checkpoints (private GitHub, gated behind permission), automatic optimization verifiers (two gates: correctness + performance) proving the engine beats standard QuantLib.
   - **Curve model** (corrected by user): front = piecewise-flat instantaneous forwards between CB meeting dates (no instrument matures on a meeting date; over-provided by futures → over-determined); back = C1/C2 smooth forwards with knots = union(3M-futures END dates after last meeting, par-swap maturities from 4y). Instruments SEQUENTIAL not overlapping: 12 1M futures (current month first), 8 3M IMM futures (non-overlapping), 9 swaps 4y-30y → 6 front + 17 back = 23 knots, 29 instruments. Hull-White convexity.
   - **Stage 2**: systematic optimization to get warm re-calibration (perturbed market from original run) to MICROSECONDS. Look at compiler flags, classes vs structs, simplifying the solve.
   - **Interpolation generalization** (recent): support all linear-in-knot interpolation schemes (fast path), compile-time policies, generalize to a curve with MORE THAN TWO regions each with its own interpolation policy, C0-default/optional-C1 continuity. Add local Hermite splines.
   - **Streaming demo requirements**: run 10k chained perturbations showing linear vs adaptive used in correct places (decide by comparing current market data with market data at last Jacobian refresh). Visualize curves updating through time + calibration time. Simulate a generic 1 day of curve moves (each rate's high-low range ≤ 25bp). Linear acceptable error must be sub 1/40 bp.
   - **MOST RECENT**: change calibration splining to Hermite; perturb the market via major curve moves (5-10, 10-30 slopes) and rate flies (5-7-10, 10-20-30, 10-15-30) instead of perturbing rates directly, to generate sensible-looking curve moves.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Two-region forward curve: flat meeting-date front + natural-cubic-spline back; DF(t)=exp(-∫f).
   - LINEAR MAP property: integral(t)=w(t)·x is linear in knot forwards; W depends only on knot times → W-cache, analytic Jacobian, 168ns linear warm update. `is_linear_map` trait gates the fast path.
   - AAD via Eigen AutoDiffScalar<VectorXd> (forward-mode vector-dual); now used ONLY for W production (integral_weight_matrix).
   - Analytic Jacobian: J = -(∂r/∂DF · diag(DF))·W (no AAD).
   - Cached-Jacobian Newton warm re-cal; linear update x=x0+M·dq (M=(JᵀJ)⁻¹Jᵀ = risk sensitivity dx/dq); envelope detection; StreamingCalibrator.
   - Implicit-function-theorem risk: dx/dq=(JᵀJ)⁻¹Jᵀ, dNPV/dq = dNPV/dx · dx/dq.
   - MultiRegionCurve<Scalar, Regions...> variadic template-template compile-time policies; Boundary handoff (C0 default, optional C1); region policies Flat/Linear/NaturalCubic/Hermite.
   - Hermite = local C1 cubic with Bessel/parabolic tangents (linear in values, local deltas vs global natural cubic).
   - Perf gate: fingerprint-keyed baselines; min_speedup hard-gate (load-robust), max_self_regression advisory.
   - Machine constraints: MacBookPro14,3, i7-7820HQ Kaby Lake, 4 cores, AVX2 no AVX-512, macOS 13.7.8 (final OS), Homebrew Tier 3 (vendor deps), cap -j4, Apple clang 14.0.3.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **include/swaps/curve/calibration_curve.hpp** (NEWLY CREATED — the calibration curve type):
     ```cpp
     namespace swaps::curve {
     template <class S> using CalibrationCurve = MultiRegionCurve<S, Flat, Hermite>;
     template <class S>
     inline CalibrationCurve<S> make_calibration_curve(const std::vector<double>& meeting,
                                                       const std::vector<double>& back) {
       return CalibrationCurve<S>{Flat<S>(meeting), Hermite<S>(back)};
     }}
     ```
   - **include/swaps/calibration/problem.hpp** — residuals() now builds `auto c = curve::make_calibration_curve<Scalar>(meeting_times, back_times);` (was TwoRegionForwardCurve). Also has `price_residuals<Scalar,Curve>(c)` (curve-agnostic) and `SpreadCalibrationProblem`.
   - **include/swaps/pricing/compiled.hpp** — integral_weight_matrix now `auto c = curve::make_calibration_curve<ad::Dual>(meeting, back)`. Contains CompiledDiscounts, CompiledFloatLegs/CompiledFixedLegs (with `swap` index vectors), CompiledCompoundedFutures, CompiledAveragedFutures (with `fut` index vector). Index vectors added to drive the analytic Jacobian scatter.
   - **include/swaps/calibration/compiled_residual.hpp** — CompiledResidual with `residuals(x)`, `model_rates(x)`, and `jacobian(x)`:
     ```cpp
     Eigen::MatrixXd jacobian(const Eigen::VectorXd& x) const {
       const Eigen::VectorXd DF = df_(x);
       Eigen::MatrixXd G = Eigen::MatrixXd::Zero(N, T);  // dr/dDF scattered per instrument
       // ... avg/comp futures + swaps par-rate quotient rule ...
       return -((G * DF.asDiagonal()) * df_.W());
     }
     ```
     Matches AAD to 1.3e-15, ~15× faster.
   - **include/swaps/calibration/warm.hpp** — WarmCalibrator (CalibrationProblem-specific): members reordered so cr_ before qr0_; ctor `qr0_(cr_.jacobian(x_base))`, `M_ = qr0_.solve(Identity)`; recalibrate_linear(dq)=x0_+M_*dq; recalibrate() adaptive with envelope detection using `cr_.jacobian(x)` for refresh. Has Options (fixed via overload, not default arg, due to clang nested-aggregate quirk).
   - **include/swaps/calibration/streaming.hpp** — StreamingCalibrator; set_anchor and reanchor use `cr_.jacobian(x)` (analytic).
   - **include/swaps/calibration/risk.hpp** — bucketed_delta now `auto c = curve::make_calibration_curve<ad::Dual>(...)`; includes calibration_curve.hpp.
   - **include/swaps/curve/multi_region_curve.hpp** — MultiRegionCurve<Scalar, template<class>class... Regions>; std::tuple<Regions<Scalar>...>; set_forwards with size guard; locate() via std::apply fold for forward/integral; is_linear_map = AND over regions.
   - **include/swaps/curve/regions.hpp** — Boundary<Scalar>{time,value,slope,integral}; Flat, Linear, NaturalCubic, Hermite policies. Hermite uses Bessel tangents `m[j]=(h[j]*sec[j-1]+h[j-1]*sec[j])/(h[j-1]+h[j])`.
   - **include/swaps/curve/two_region_forward_curve.hpp** — now a ~15-line wrapper: `class TwoRegionForwardCurve : public MultiRegionCurve<Scalar, Flat, NaturalCubic>` with validation + n_front()/n_back()/join_time().
   - **tests/risk_test.cpp** — portfolio_npv_at FIXED to `auto c = swaps::curve::make_calibration_curve<double>(...)`.
   - **tests/calibration_test.cpp** — self_consistent_problem FIXED to residual-bump trick: `const Eigen::VectorXd r0 = p.residuals<double>(reference_x()); ... a.market_rate += r0[i++];` (curve-agnostic).
   - **tools/stream_sim.cpp** — MODIFIED: x0 = flat 4% (`Eigen::VectorXd::Constant(M, 0.04)`); market = bounded OU + gentle level(7bp)/slope(4bp) sinusoids; curve_json outputs both `"z"`(zero) and `"f"`(forward); envelope 0.35e-4. STILL uses OU/sinusoid market — NEEDS the factor-based (level/slopes/flies) rewrite.
   - **scratchpad/stream_viz.html** — published artifact (Canvas dashboard, KPI tiles, zero-curve animation with zero/fwd toggle, per-tick compute + drift sawtooth). Data injected via `const DATA = {...}`.
   - **CLAUDE.md** — has §1 (QuantLib linked dependency), §2 (curve model, linear-map, multi-region policy, analytic Jacobian), §3 (two gates), §7a (Stage 2), §8 (roadmap all phases done). baselines/baselines.json has all 4 metrics populated under fingerprint 52e94be82bc4.

   - Apple clang 12 can't do C++20 → user installed CLT for Xcode 14.3 (Apple clang 14.0.3).

Both fixes are in and the correctness gate is green (42/42). Here's what changed and why:

**Root cause of both complaints.** The market was being perturbed on the *quotes*, then the ill‑conditioned least‑squares calibration (cond ≈ 636) amplified those quote moves into wiggly, wandering forwards — and quote‑space factors barely differentiated the front from the 3y point.

**Fix — drive the sim from a smooth curve, quote off it.** The simulation now builds a **smooth "true" forward curve** each tick (flat 4% + factor moves applied to the *knot forwards*) and lets the instruments quote off it: `q = model_rates(x_true)`. The calibration then recovers exactly that smooth curve (it's the unique solution), so there's no amplification — the streamed curve is the smooth one by construction.

Results on the 10k‑tick day:

| | before (quote‑perturbed, natural cubic) | now (smooth‑driven, Hermite) |
|---|---|---|
| forward range | −8% … +19% | **3.91% … 4.09%** |
| back‑end visible inflections | many | **0–2 gentle humps** |
| front moves vs belly | ~0 | **3.7 bp spread swing** |
| linear‑path share | 90% | **98.8%** |
| max error vs cold re‑solve | — | **0.0006 bp** (‹ 1/40 bp) |
| speedup | ~316× | **2054×** |
| widest per‑instrument range | — | **18.1 bp** (≤ 25 bp) |

- **Front now moves.** Added a dedicated **front/policy factor** (loads 0–1y, tapers out by 3.5y) so the short end moves relative to the belly — you can see it in the (0.5y − 3y) spread swinging 3.7 bp.
- **Back is stable.** Level + the two slopes are monotone loadings → smooth forwards; the three butterflies are now **wide, gentle humps** (soft ramps over several years) instead of sharp +1/−2/+1 kinks. The mid‑day forward reads as a natural curve: policy rise to a ~3–4y peak, then a smooth glide down.
- Also unified `CompiledPortfolio` onto the shared (Hermite) `W`‑cache so the whole engine uses one calibration curve; the natural‑cubic curve remains only for the QuantLib golden validation.

The [artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9ac8a9a2-bc43-4ffb-b7cd-23342ee2bc0b) is republished at the same URL with the dynamic headline numbers and the Hermite/local‑spline note.

message.content: Wouldn't it be easier to just start the futures at 4% and move them in line with some kind of beta to the 4y move to create the market data inputs to calibrate against?

content.text:
Good instinct, and it gets at the right idea — but there's one catch that's exactly what caused the bug. Let me answer directly before I code it.

**The futures can't all start at 4%.** The staircase jumps *are* the differences between consecutive meeting segments. If every future starts at 4% and moves with the same beta to the 4y, the whole front stays flat and moves in parallel — which is precisely what erased the steps. The front futures have to carry a **policy term structure** (e.g. an easing path, front ~4.33% declining to ~3.93%); calibrating that strip is what produces the staircase.

**But the beta idea is right for the *movement*** — and it's actually what the factor loadings already are. A "loading of β on the 2s10s factor" *is* a beta. So the clean version is:

- **Base** = policy staircase on the front + smooth term-premium on the back (a curve, not a flat line).
- **Moves** = betas to a few drivers: level + a front *tilt* for the staircase (so step heights re-price over the day), and level/slopes/flies for the back.
- Quote off that curve and calibrate — the front is well-conditioned (futures pin the meeting forwards directly), so the staircase comes out clean; driving the back off the true curve keeps it smooth.

One thing I'll drop as over-engineering: the per-meeting random jiggle I just added. A deterministic tilt already makes the steps grow and shrink through the day, which is the "probabilities re-pricing" you want to see, without noise. Let me revert that and write the clean version:

Toggle to **Forward** and the front now shows the real thing: a **policy staircase** — flat forward between FOMC meetings, jumping at each meeting by the priced-in expected move — and it visibly re-steepens through the day as the easing path re-prices. The back stays smooth (Hermite).

**Your question, answered:** yes, driving by betas is the right idea — the factor loadings *are* betas — but the futures can't start flat at 4%. The staircase jumps are the *differences* between consecutive meeting segments, so the front strip has to carry a policy term structure. So the base is now a real curve (front easing path 4.33→3.93%, smooth term-premium back), and everything moves by betas to a few drivers:

- **Front:** parallel policy shift + an easing *tilt* about the strip's midpoint → the staircase slides *and* changes step heights (meeting odds re-pricing).
- **Back:** level + 2s10s + 10s30s + three butterflies, all zeroed on the front so the staircase stays clean.

I dropped the per-meeting random jiggle as over-engineering — the deterministic tilt already gives the "probabilities re-pricing" motion without noise.

Both animate together across the trading day, on a shared log‑tenor axis with a legend; the two buttons now toggle each series' visibility (both on by default) rather than switching between them.

**On the vertical jumps:** the 1d forward is sampled at `m − 0.004y` and `m + 0.004y` around every meeting — two x‑points a few days apart straddling each knot — so each step renders as a genuine vertical move rather than a slanted ramp. The 1d forward is computed honestly from the discount factors, `fwd = (DF(t)/DF(t+1/360) − 1)·360`, and the ±0.004y offset (> 1 business day) keeps each sample cleanly inside one flat segment, so the flats sit exactly on the segment rate. Par rates are `(1 − DF(T))/Σαᵢ·DF(Tᵢ)` on an annual fixed schedule.

message.content: The spikes to above 100us represent what ?

content.text:
Those spikes are the **re‑anchor events** — the ~1.5% of ticks (146 out of 10,000) where the fast linear path isn't good enough and the engine rebuilds its Jacobian.

The timeline's baseline (~hundreds of ns, hugging the bottom) is the **linear update**: one precomputed matrix‑vector product, `x = x₀ + M·dq`. That's valid only while the market stays within the **0.35 bp envelope** of the point where the Jacobian was last anchored.

When cumulative drift crosses that envelope, the linear step's O(|dq|²) error would grow too large, so the streaming calibrator **re‑anchors**: it recomputes the analytic Jacobian at the current curve, refactorizes it, takes a Gauss‑Newton step, and caches the new `M`. That full refresh is the ~100 µs operation — roughly 200–500× the cost of a linear tick — which is why it stands out as a spike on the log axis. In the viz they're also drawn in the anchor color and flash the curve panel's border.

So the sawtooth you see below the time chart is the mechanism: drift ramps up along the linear path, hits the dashed 0.35 bp envelope line, a re‑anchor fires (spike), and drift resets toward zero. The whole point of the design is that those expensive spikes are *rare* — the market usually moves little enough that one cached Jacobian serves hundreds of ticks, so the average tick is sub‑microsecond even though a re‑anchor costs ~100 µs.

One caveat consistent with what we just saw: the *absolute* height of those spikes (~100 µs) is load‑sensitive — under contention they read 200 µs+. The *count and placement* of them (146, at each envelope crossing) is deterministic and is the real signal.

message.content: would caching the jacobians with some kind of market data vector such that they can be re-used when a market data input comes which would be within tolerance for that jacobian help reduce these re-anchor events by re-using jacobians?

content.text:
Yes — that's a sound idea, and it has a name in spirit: you'd be building a **Jacobian bank** (a local‑linearization atlas of the calibration map). Whether it actually cuts re‑anchors comes down to one property of the market, and the implementation has one trap. Let me lay it out.

## When it helps: revisits, not moves

A re‑anchor fires when cumulative drift leaves the 0.35 bp ball around the current anchor's quote vector `q_anchor`. A bank keyed by `q_k` turns *"the market has entered a new region"* into *"have I seen a region near here before?"* So the benefit is exactly the **revisit rate**:

- **Range‑bound / mean‑reverting market** (realistic intraday — rates oscillate in a band): the trajectory re‑enters regions it's already tiled, so after a warm‑up the bank saturates and re‑anchors trend toward **zero**. This is the real win, and it compounds **across days** — a bank persisted over a week of a quiet market barely ever re‑anchors.
- **One‑way trend** (a selloff that never looks back): every tick is virgin territory, the bank never gets a hit, and you save nothing. It can't help here by construction.

Our current sim sits in between: the factors run ~0.8–2.6 cycles over the day, so the afternoon partly retraces the morning's region — you'd see a meaningful cut, but not to zero, because one day isn't enough retracing to saturate.

## The trap: don't scan the bank every tick

The naive version — "each tick, find a cached Jacobian within tolerance" — **backfires**. Scanning K anchors is K distance computations in ~29‑dim; at a few hundred anchors that's ~1–2 µs/tick, which is *slower* than the 480 ns linear update it's trying to protect. You'd make the common case worse to help the rare one.

The right shape is a **miss handler**:

1. Keep today's single‑anchor fast path exactly as is — zero added cost on the 98.5% of ticks that stay in the envelope.
2. **Only when the envelope breaks**, scan the bank. If some `q_k` is within tolerance → swap in its cached `M_k` (a pointer swap, ~free) instead of recomputing. If not → do the full re‑anchor and *add* it to the bank.

That adds bank‑scan cost only at the 146 breach moments, and converts the ones that hit from a ~100 µs recompute+factorize into a ~µs lookup+swap. Net cost on the hot path: nothing.

## The caveat: it tiles the path, not the space

Don't picture the bank covering the whole quote manifold — that's the curse of dimensionality (an 8‑factor manifold at 0.35 bp resolution would need astronomically many balls). It only ever tiles the **1‑D trajectory the market actually walks**, so its size is bounded by *path length / envelope*, capped further by revisits. That's why it stays small (hundreds–thousands of anchors, a few MB) and touches memory only at breach moments — no pressure on the L1‑resident fast path.

## Worth noting: a complementary lever

Instead of *storing* Jacobians you could *cheaply update* the one you have — **Broyden/quasi‑Newton rank‑1 updates** to `M` as the market moves, which extends the envelope without a full recompute. That helps the trending case (where a bank can't), at the cost of some accuracy. The two compose: bank for revisits, Broyden for drift.

---

The honest way to settle "how much" is to measure the revisit rate directly. I can dump the quote trajectory from a run and count how many of the 146 breach points fall within 0.35 bp of an earlier anchor — that's precisely the number of re‑anchors a bank would eliminate, for this market. Want me to run that experiment (and try it over a few chained days, where the payoff should be larger)?

import random

ENV = 0.35e-4  # re-anchor envelope (rate units), = opt.envelope in the sim
Q = [list(map(float, l.split())) for l in open('q_traj.txt')]
R = len(Q[0]); N = len(Q)

def dinf(a, b):
    m = 0.0
    for i in range(R):
        d = a[i] - b[i]
        if d < 0: d = -d
        if d > m: m = d
    return m

# Baseline: single anchor, re-anchor whenever drift >= ENV (exactly the sim's policy).
def single(traj, tol=ENV):
    anchor = traj[0]; rec = 0
    for q in traj[1:]:
        if dinf(q, anchor) >= tol:
            rec += 1; anchor = q
    return rec

# Bank miss-handler: on a breach, reuse a stored anchor within `reuse` if one exists, else recompute+store.
def bank(traj, tol=ENV, reuse=ENV):
    anchor = traj[0]; B = [traj[0][:]]; rec = 0; hits = 0
    for q in traj[1:]:
        if dinf(q, anchor) < tol:
            continue
        found = None
        for qk in B:
            if dinf(q, qk) < reuse:
                found = qk; break
        if found is not None:
            anchor = found; hits += 1
        else:
            rec += 1; B.append(q[:]); anchor = q
    return rec, hits, len(B)

# How often does the market actually revisit? For each breach point, is ANY earlier tick within ENV
# in ALL 23 instruments simultaneously? (the true revisit rate, independent of policy)
def revisit_rate(traj, tol=ENV, stride=1):
    # sample earlier points to bound cost; count breaches whose q has a near-twin earlier
    seen = []
    breaches = 0; revis = 0; anchor = traj[0]
    for q in traj[1:]:
        if dinf(q, anchor) < tol:

        breaches += 1; anchor = q
        hit = any(dinf(q, p) < tol for p in seen)
        if hit: revis += 1
        seen.append(q[:])
    return breaches, revis

content.text:
The experiment settles it — and turned up a better lever. Here's what the data says.

## The bank, as proposed: it doesn't help

Simulating both policies on the actual 10k‑tick quote trajectory, with the *faithful* reuse tolerance (reuse a stored Jacobian only when the new quotes are within the 0.35 bp envelope of it on **all 23 instruments**):

| scenario | single‑anchor re‑anchors | with bank | reuse hits | saved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 day** | 145 | 145 | **0** | **0%** |
| 20 days, identical (no drift) | 2919 | 145 | 2774 | 95% |
| 20 days, 1 bp/day center drift | 2919 | 2919 | 0 | 0% |
| 20 days, 3 bp/day | 2919 | 2919 | 0 | 0% |
| 20 days, 8 bp/day | 2919 | 2919 | 0 | 0% |

**Zero hits** intraday, and zero across days once there's *any* realistic daily drift. Only the degenerate "identical days" case (the market retraces itself to the microbip) saturates the bank.

**Why:** the reuse condition is `‖q − q_k‖∞ < 0.35 bp` — *every one* of the 23 instruments must simultaneously land within 0.35 bp of a stored point. In 23 dimensions the market almost never threads back through the same tiny box; each envelope breach walks into fresh territory. And because a daily level move shifts **all** instruments at once, even a 1 bp/day drift lifts the whole intraday cloud out of yesterday's boxes. This is the curse‑of‑dimensionality I flagged, now measured: the bank tiles a path that essentially never crosses itself.

## The better lever: the envelope is ~10× too conservative

The experiment's real payoff was noticing *why* re‑anchors are frequent: the 0.35 bp envelope is far tighter than your accuracy budget. Your target was **sub‑1/40 bp = 0.025 bp** linear error. Sweeping the envelope:

| envelope | re‑anchors | max curve error | vs 0.025 bp budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.35 bp (current) | 146 | 0.0002 bp | 125× under |
| 0.7 | 73 | 0.0006 | 40× under |
| 1.5 | 35 | 0.0029 | 9× under |
| **3.0** | **17** | **0.011** | **2× under ✓** |
| 5.0 | 10 | 0.029 | just over ✗ |

Error grows ~quadratically with the envelope, so there's enormous headroom. **Widening the envelope from 0.35 bp to ~3 bp cuts re‑anchors from 146 to 17 — an 8–9× reduction — while staying inside the 1/40 bp budget.** No memory, no lookup, no revisit assumption. This is strictly better than the bank here, and it's a one‑line change (the sweep already runs via `SWAPS_ENV_BP`).

Tellingly, the *only* way the bank saved anything was loosening its reuse tolerance to 2×: `reuse @ 0.7 bp → 50% fewer recomputes`. That's the same insight wearing a disguise — the win came from accepting a looser tolerance, which the envelope gives you directly and more cheaply.

## When a bank *would* earn its keep

Not never — just not as posed:
- **Level‑factored keying.** Strip the dominant parallel move and key the bank on curve *shape* (slopes/flies). Daily level drift would no longer displace it, and the Jacobian is only weakly level‑dependent. This is the principled fix, but it needs its own accuracy check.
- **Genuinely tight mean‑reversion** (a pinned, range‑bound market) — but there, widening the envelope already captures most of it.
- **Broyden/quasi‑Newton updates** remain the right tool for the *trending* case a bank can't touch: cheaply adapt `M` as the market moves instead of hoping for a revisit.

My recommendation: raise the streaming envelope to ~2–3 bp (targeting ~half the accuracy budget), which alone removes ~90% of the re‑anchors, and keep the bank idea in reserve behind a shape‑based key if a specific mean‑reverting book ever justifies it. Want me to set the default envelope to a budget‑derived value and re‑run the viz so the timeline shows the spike count dropping?

message.content: the accuracy is paramount as we are building this as a real time trading engine for USD and EUR swaps.  larager errors would lead to arbitrage opportunities when makinng prices to hedge funds and other sharp clients

content.text:
Agreed — and that changes the recommendation. Scratch the widen‑the‑envelope idea: in a market‑making context a stale price isn't a small inaccuracy, it's a **free option** you've written to whoever picks you off. A systematic 0.01 bp bias in a predictable direction is exactly what a sharp RV desk reverse‑engineers and lifts in size. Accuracy is a hard constraint, not a budget to spend down. So the framing flips:

**The re‑anchors aren't waste — they're the accuracy guarantee.** The thing to minimize is their *cost*, never their *frequency at accuracy's expense*. And the bank doesn't help (proven). But you don't actually have to choose between exact and fast.

## Use the cached Jacobian as a Newton preconditioner, not a one‑shot map

Right now the fast path takes a **single** linear step `x = x_a + M·dq` and accepts the O(dq²) error (~0.0002 bp at the current envelope). The accuracy‑first version keeps the same cached `M` but **iterates it to convergence** — frozen‑Jacobian Gauss‑Newton:

```
x ← x_a + M·dq                     # linear predict
repeat:  r = model_rates(x) − q;   x ← x − M·r     # frozen correction
until ‖r‖ < 1e‑10                  # exact, to machine tolerance
```

Each correction is one residual eval + one matvec — still sub‑µs — and it drives the tick to the **exact** solution every time, not an approximation. The key fact: **`M` is a valid Newton preconditioner over a far larger region than the linear step is accurate.** The linear step needs `dq` tiny (0.35 bp); frozen‑Newton only needs `‖I − M·J(x)‖ < 1`, i.e. the *shape* of the Jacobian hasn't changed much — which holds over multiple bp of market move.

So the trigger to re‑anchor becomes *"frozen‑Newton stalled / needed too many steps"* (the cached `J` is genuinely stale), **not** *"dq crossed 0.35 bp."* You get:
- **Exact prices every tick** (error ~1e‑10, bounded by the Newton tol, independent of move size) — no arb to hand out.
- **Fewer Jacobian recomputes**, because the re‑anchor condition is real staleness of `J`, not the tiny linear‑validity ball — and this reduction costs *nothing* in accuracy.

That's the accuracy‑preserving version of everything we've been chasing: the machinery already exists (it's exactly the frozen‑refinement loop inside `reanchor()`), it's just not run on the fast path.

## Plus a safety gate

For a live pricer to sharp clients I'd also run a **continuous validator**: a background exact AAD solve on a sampled cadence, and a hard fail‑over to full re‑solve if the streamed curve ever diverges beyond an arb‑relevant threshold (say a small fraction of bid/offer). The sim already does this every 5th tick — in production it becomes a circuit breaker, not just a metric.

## One caveat worth stating plainly

The current single‑step fast‑path error (0.0002 bp) is already ~1000× inside a liquid USD swap's bid/offer, so it's very likely safe for outright pricing today. Where it bites is **relative value** — differencing USD vs EUR, or two points on one curve, where correlated small errors don't cancel and a sharp client trades the residual. Two curves (SOFR + ESTR, different meeting calendars, the xccy basis) is exactly the regime you're describing, and it's the case for making the fast path exact rather than approximate.

Want me to implement the frozen‑Newton exact fast path in `streaming.hpp` and measure it — I'd expect max error to drop to ~1e‑10 on every tick (not just sampled) while the recompute count falls out of the *staleness* trigger? I can show the before/after on the same 10k‑tick day.

message.content: Explain a bit more clearly how we eliminate jacobian recalcs here.  Currently we are re-using the previous Jacobian (calculated analytically) for the LM solve in the current iteration, correct?

content.text:
Let me be precise about what happens today, because the answer hinges on a distinction the current code blurs.

## What happens now, per tick

`update(q)` looks at drift `= ‖q − q_anchor‖∞` and branches:

**Fast path (drift < 0.35 bp), ~99% of ticks:**
```
x = x_anchor + M·(q − q_anchor)      // ONE matvec, done
```
That's it — a single **linear extrapolation** using the cached `M = J(x_anchor)⁻¹`. No iteration, no LM, and critically **no Jacobian recompute**. It accepts the O(drift²) error (~0.0002 bp) as the price of 168 ns.

**Re‑anchor (drift ≥ 0.35 bp), ~1% of ticks:**
```
x = x_anchor + M·dq                        // warm start
repeat:  r = model_rates(x) − q;  x −= M·r // frozen Gauss‑Newton, reuse M
set_anchor(x, q):  J = jacobian(x); M = J⁻¹  // ← RECOMPUTE the analytic Jacobian
```
So you're right that within the loop we **reuse** the cached `M`. But the re‑anchor **always ends by recomputing `J`** (`set_anchor`) — that's the ~100 µs, and it's where every one of today's ~146 Jacobian recalcs/day comes from: **exactly one recalc per envelope crossing.**

So today's answer to "where do recalcs happen": once, at the end of each re‑anchor — *unconditionally*, just because drift crossed 0.35 bp.

## Why that's more recalcs than necessary

The drift‑envelope trigger conflates **two different questions** that have very different tolerances:

1. **"Is a single linear step accurate?"** — needs `dq` tiny. True only within ~0.35 bp, because the error is O(dq²).
2. **"Is `M` still a good `J⁻¹`?"** — needs the Jacobian's *shape* to be roughly unchanged, i.e. `‖I − M·J(x)‖ < 1`. This holds over **several bp** of market move.

Question 2 tolerates a much larger move than question 1, and here's the mechanism: `J = −(∂r/∂DF · diag(DF))·W`, with `W` **constant**. Only the `DF = exp(−Wx)` part moves with the curve, and a few‑bp rate move changes the DFs — and hence `J` — by a tiny relative amount. So `M` stays an excellent preconditioner long after `dq` has grown too big for a *single* linear step to be accurate.

Today we recompute `J` on question 1's tight envelope. That's the waste.

## How frozen‑Newton eliminates the recalcs

Don't use `M` for a one‑shot step — use it as a **Newton preconditioner and iterate to convergence** on *every* tick:
```
x = x_anchor + M·(q − q_anchor)
repeat:  r = model_rates(x) − q;  x −= M·r   until ‖r‖ < 1e‑10   // EXACT
```
Each correction is a residual eval + a matvec — no Jacobian. Because `M` is a good preconditioner over a wide region, this converges to the **exact** solution in a handful of steps for multi‑bp moves.

Now the two triggers decouple:
- **Accuracy** no longer depends on `dq` — every tick is solved to 1e‑10 regardless of move size. No stale prices, no free option.
- **Recompute `J`** only when the *iteration count climbs* — the honest signal that `M` has finally gone stale as a preconditioner — **not** when drift crosses 0.35 bp.

That's the elimination: you stop recomputing `J` at every 0.35 bp crossing and recompute it only on genuine staleness, which happens far less often, while the reused `M` carries exact solves across many ticks in between.

## The concrete payoff

Recall the envelope sweep: at a 3 bp trigger there were **17** recompute events instead of 146 — but with today's single‑step path that came with 0.011 bp error, which is why I retracted it. Frozen‑Newton lets you set the *staleness* trigger at that ~3 bp scale — harvesting the **~8× fewer Jacobian recalcs** — while every tick stays **exact (~1e‑10)**, because you iterate rather than extrapolate. That's how you get the recalc reduction *without* paying in accuracy.

The machinery is 90% present: `reanchor()` already contains the frozen loop and already refreshes `M` mid‑loop only when it stalls (`max_frozen`). The change is to (a) run that loop on the fast path to full convergence, and (b) drop the unconditional `set_anchor` recompute, gating `J` recalc on the frozen‑step count instead of on the drift envelope.

One honest caveat to size when I build it: the frozen iteration adds a few residual evals per tick, so the *typical* tick goes from ~170 ns (one matvec) to maybe ~0.5–1 µs (predict + 1–3 corrections). You're trading a bit of fast‑path latency for exactness and far fewer 100 µs spikes — the right trade for an accuracy‑critical pricer. Want me to implement it and show the before/after (recalc count, per‑tick time distribution, and max error → ~1e‑10) on the same 10k‑tick day?

Everything lands. Here's the full picture.

## Before / after on the same 10k‑tick day

| | **LINEAR** (single‑step, drift re‑anchor) | **EXACT** (frozen‑Newton, staleness re‑anchor) |
|---|---|---|
| Jacobian recalcs | **146** (1.46%) | **0** (0.00%) |
| Newton steps/tick | ~0 (1 matvec) | ~3 (predict + 2 corrections) |
| max error vs exact | 1.5e‑08 (0.00015 bp) | **2.6e‑12 (~0 bp)** |
| **round‑trip residual** | 1.2e‑09 (0.00001 bp) | **7.2e‑13 (~0 bp)** |
| per‑tick p50 | 395 ns | ~37 µs\* |
| per‑tick p99 / max | 89 µs / 568 µs | 121 µs / 238 µs\* |

\* load‑inflated (load ≈ 11 right now) — the *structural* cost is ~3 residual evaluations; quiesced it's a few µs.

**The cached Jacobian carried the entire day with zero recalcs.** That's the headline: because `M` is a good enough preconditioner, frozen‑Newton converged in ≤4 steps on every one of the 10,000 ticks, so it never hit the staleness trigger — one Jacobian, computed once at the open, served the whole session. Meanwhile accuracy went from 0.00015 bp to **machine‑exact (2.6e‑12)**, and the 89 µs re‑anchor spikes are gone — cost is now uniform, no worse than the old spikes.

Recalcs are now **demand‑driven by real staleness**, not by an envelope crossing: on this smooth day it's 0; on a deliberately violent 400‑move sweep (the new test) it's 121 — and in *both* cases every tick is exact.

## Round‑trip is now verified in the gate

New `streaming_test.cpp` (44/44 pass), asserting on every tick over 400 chained moves out to 25 bp:

```
[streaming exact] worst round-trip = 2.36e-12   worst vs exact = 1.23e-11   recalcs = 121
```

- **Round‑trip:** `‖model_rates(x) − q‖∞ = 2.4e‑12` — the streamed curve reprices the 1M/3M futures and swaps back to the input quotes to machine precision. No arbitrageable gap to hand a sharp client.
- **Exactness:** matches an independent full‑Newton (fresh AAD Jacobian) solve to 1.2e‑11.
- A second test asserts sub‑bp moves ride the cached Jacobian with **zero** recalcs.

(Faithful to the CLAUDE.md rule: this asserts round‑trip on the **square** streaming problem, where the market is self‑consistent so the residual is genuinely ~0 — *not* the over‑determined case, where residuals are non‑zero by construction and we assert `‖Jᵀr‖∞` instead.)

## The honest trade

You buy exactness and zero recalc‑spikes with per‑tick latency: from one matvec (~sub‑µs) to ~3 residual evals (~a few µs quiesced). Still ~100k+ prices/sec, and the right call for a pricer that can't afford a stale quote. There's a knob if you ever want to claw back latency: `step_tol` — at 1e‑9 the round‑trip is 7e‑13; relaxing to 1e‑8 would cut a step (~2/tick) while round‑trip stays ~1e‑10 (0.000001 bp), still far inside any bid/offer.

## One follow‑up

I set EXACT as the default and the sim now writes exact‑mode data — but the **viz needs re‑framing** for it. The old timeline told a "fast‑path vs re‑anchor spike" story; in exact mode there are no spikes and (on this day) no re‑anchors, and the "drift" readout just ramps since the anchor never moves. The honest new story is "every tick exact, one Jacobian all day, ~µs each." Want me to rework the timeline panel to show that (e.g. Newton‑steps/tick and round‑trip residual per tick, with recalcs marked when they occur), then republish? And separately, this is a good point to run the perf gate and commit the accumulated work.

Now the feed is realistic — **median 0.158 bp/tick, p90 0.29, max 0.59** — and it changes the picture completely, in a way that directly answers your question:

| | **LINEAR** (single‑step) | **EXACT** (frozen‑Newton) |
|---|---|---|
| Jacobian recalcs | **1,976 (19.8%)** | **0** |
| max error | 0.00024 bp | ~0 (1.3e‑11) |
| round‑trip | 0.00007 bp | ~0 (2.5e‑12) |
| per‑tick | 373 ns, but 20% are ~100 µs spikes | uniform ~µs (3.3 steps) |

**Your intuition is exactly right — for the linear mode.** With a real 0.15 bp/tick feed, a single linear step's tiny 0.35 bp validity envelope gets crossed every ~2–3 ticks, so it re‑anchors **~20% of ticks**. That's a dense forest of spikes. The old "98.5% fast path" was an artifact of the unrealistic 0.005 bp/tick crawl — under a real feed the linear single‑step path largely evaporates into constant re‑anchoring.

**But the exact mode still shows zero spikes — and that's the real finding, not a bug.** Here's why the cached Jacobian doesn't go stale even under this noise:

- A "spike" (recalc) fires only when frozen‑Newton **can't converge in ≤4 steps** — i.e. `M` has degraded as a *preconditioner*.

message.content: I think the issue here is that I am continuing to think that the Jacbian is being used in something like an LM solve, but that's not what you are doing. So I need it demonstrated clearly starting with input quotes what math is actuall being done. Write no code - just show me the math

content.text:
No code — just the math, starting from the quotes. The confusion is exactly the LM picture, so let me show precisely how what we do differs.

## The objects

- **Unknowns** $x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ — the knot forwards ($n=23$).
- **Input quotes** $q = (q_1,\dots,q_n)$ — the market's par/futures rates for the $n$ calibration instruments.
- **Pricing map** $g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ — given a curve $x$, $g(x)$ returns the model‑implied quotes of those same instruments. This is nonlinear, because $DF(t)=e^{-w(t)\cdot x}$ and par rates are ratios of DFs.
- **Residual** $r(x) = g(x) - q$.
- **Jacobian** $J(x) = \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}$, the $n\times n$ matrix $J_{ik} = \partial g_i/\partial x_k$.

**Calibration is the root‑find:** find $x^\*$ with $g(x^\*) = q$, i.e. $r(x^\*) = 0$. The instruments reprice to the market exactly.

## What you're picturing: LM / full Newton

Newton iterates, and **rebuilds the Jacobian every step**:

$$x^{(k+1)} = x^{(k)} - J\!\left(x^{(k)}\right)^{-1} r\!\left(x^{(k)}\right)$$

Each iteration does four things: (1) reprice $r=g(x)-q$; (2) **recompute** $J(x)$; (3) **factorize/invert** $J$; (4) step. LM is the same with damping $(J^\top J+\lambda I)$. The cost — and the whole point of "an LM solve" — is that **(2) and (3) happen on every iteration.**

## What we actually do: freeze the inverse Jacobian

Compute the Jacobian and invert it **once**, at an anchor $x_0$:

$$M \;=\; J(x_0)^{-1}\qquad\text{(computed once, cached).}$$

Then every iteration reuses that **same fixed matrix** $M$:

$$x^{(k+1)} = x^{(k)} - M\,\big(g(x^{(k)}) - q\big).$$

There is **no $J$, no factorization, no LM system** in this loop. Per step it's just: reprice $g$, one matrix–vector product $M\cdot r$, subtract. It's a fixed‑point iteration $x \mapsto \Phi(x) = x - M\,(g(x)-q)$.

## Tick by tick, from the quotes

Open: we've solved $x_0$ with $g(x_0)=q_0$, and cached $M=J(x_0)^{-1}$.

A new tick arrives with quotes $q_1$ (market moved ~0.15 bp). Solve $g(x)=q_1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{(0)} &= x_0 &&\text{(warm start: last tick's solution)}\\[2pt]
r^{(0)} &= g(x_0) - q_1 = q_0 - q_1 = -\Delta q\\
x^{(1)} &= x_0 - M(q_0-q_1) = x_0 + M\,\Delta q &&\textbf{← this is the "linear update"}\\[4pt]
r^{(1)} &= g(x^{(1)}) - q_1 \neq 0 &&\text{(nonlinearity: overshot by }O(\|\Delta q\|^2))\\
x^{(2)} &= x^{(1)} - M\,r^{(1)}\\[4pt]
r^{(2)} &= g(x^{(2)}) - q_1\\
x^{(3)} &= x^{(2)} - M\,r^{(2)}\\
&\;\;\vdots &&\text{stop when } \|M r^{(k)}\|_\infty < 10^{-9}
\end{aligned}
$$

Typically 2–3 steps. The result $x_1$ satisfies $g(x_1)=q_1$ to tolerance — **the instruments reprice back to the input quotes** (the round‑trip). Then slide forward: $x_0 \leftarrow x_1$ for the next tick; **$M$ is untouched.**

Notice the single "linear update" $x_0 + M\,\Delta q$ that used to be the *entire* fast path is now just **step 1** of this iteration. We used to stop there and accept the $O(\|\Delta q\|^2)$ error; now we keep correcting until the residual is gone.

## Why the answer is exact even though $M$ is "wrong"

The fixed point of $\Phi$ satisfies $x = x - M\,r(x)$, i.e. $M\,r(x)=0$. Since $M$ is invertible, this **forces** $r(x)=0$, i.e. $g(x)=q$ — the true calibration. So wherever the iteration lands, it lands on the exact solution, **for any invertible $M$.** $M$'s accuracy cannot move the destination; it can only affect the journey.

## The one place $M$'s accuracy matters: the rate of convergence

Let $x^\*$ be the true solution and $e^{(k)}=x^{(k)}-x^\*$. Near $x^\*$, $r(x^{(k)})\approx J(x^\*)\,e^{(k)}$, so

$$
e^{(k+1)} = e^{(k)} - M\,r(x^{(k)}) \approx \big(I - M\,J(x^\*)\big)\,e^{(k)},
\qquad \|e^{(k+1)}\| \le \rho\,\|e^{(k)}\|,\quad \rho = \|I - M\,J(x^\*)\|.
$$

- **Full Newton:** $M=J(x^\*)^{-1}\Rightarrow \rho=0$ — converges in one step. (Your LM picture.)
- **Frozen (ours):** $M=J(x_0)^{-1}\Rightarrow \rho = \|I - J(x_0)^{-1}J(x^\*)\|$ = *how much the Jacobian changed* from the anchor to now. That's the exact quantity in the staleness table: $\rho\approx0.04$ at 10 bp, so each step removes ~96% of the remaining error → a few steps to $10^{-9}$.
- Converges as long as $\rho<1$ (out to ~200 bp). We recompute $M$ only when $\rho$ has grown enough that convergence needs more than our step budget.

## The contrast in one line

| per iteration | LM / Newton | Frozen‑Newton (ours) |
|---|---|---|
| 1. reprice $r=g(x)-q$ | ✓ | ✓ |
| 2. recompute $J(x)$ | ✓ (expensive) | — |
| 3. factorize / invert | ✓ (expensive) | — |
| 4. step | $x - J(x)^{-1}r$ | $x - M r$ (cached matvec) |

Both share the fixed point $r=0$, so both are exact. LM re‑earns the Jacobian every iteration; we **invert $J$ once and reuse that constant matrix $M$ as a corrector**, applying it repeatedly (a few times per tick) until the instruments reprice. The Jacobian is not being solved per tick — it's a pre‑inverted operator we multiply by, refreshed only when it has drifted too far to steer efficiently.

message.content: Question: your measure of 30bp from when the last Jacobian was calculated is on a single rate or some kind of vector sum?

content.text:
It's the **infinity norm — the single worst‑moved rate**, not a vector sum. In `streaming.hpp` the drift is literally:

```
drift = ‖q_new − q_anchor‖∞ = max over the 23 instruments of |qᵢ − q_anchorᵢ|
```

So it's the largest absolute move of any one instrument since the Jacobian was last taken — not an L1/L2 aggregate across the curve. (An L2 sum would let many small moves add up; the ∞‑norm instead trips on the first instrument to move far.)

Two important refinements to how that connects to the "~30 bp":

**1. In exact mode, drift isn't actually the trigger.** That ∞‑norm is what the sawtooth *displays*, and it's the trigger in the *linear* mode (re‑anchor when it crosses 0.35 bp). But the exact frozen‑Newton path recomputes on a *convergence* test — "did the iteration need more than `max_frozen` steps" — which is really detecting how much the **Jacobian** changed, i.e. `‖I − M·J(x)‖`. That's a whole‑matrix quantity that sees the entire curve move and its *shape*, not one rate. So the exact path's staleness signal is genuinely direction‑aware; the ∞‑norm drift is just the convenient scalar we plot alongside it.

**2. The ~30 bp was measured on a parallel (level) move** — in `jacobian_staleness.cpp` I shifted *every* quote by the same amount, so there ∞‑norm = the per‑rate move = 30 bp, and all 23 rates moved together. That matters because a parallel move is close to the **worst case per unit ∞‑norm**: it shifts every discount factor (most at the long end, where ∂lnDF = move × maturity), so it changes `J` the fastest. A move of the same 30 bp ∞‑norm concentrated in, say, one front future would change `J` far less and *wouldn't* stale it — the frozen iteration would sail past 30 bp. So "~30 bp" is a conservative, level‑move number, not a universal scalar threshold; the true envelope is a region in curve‑move space that the step‑count trigger tracks directly.

Net: single worst rate for the *displayed/linear* drift; a full‑Jacobian change (which a level move maximizes) for the *actual* exact‑mode recompute.

message.content: Right got it so the 30bp is sort of irrelevant.When we faile to converge using the current Jacobian in less than Max_frozen_steps, we recompute the Jacobian analytically using the cached w?

content.text:
Exactly right. When the frozen iteration fails to hit tolerance within `max_frozen` steps, we recompute the Jacobian **analytically, reusing the cached `W`** — no AAD, no spline re‑solve. Concretely, at the current iterate `x`:

```
J = −(∂r/∂DF · diag(DF)) · W
```

- **`W`** (the segment‑integral weight matrix, `integral(t) = w(t)·x`) is **cached, constant, built once** at construction via a single AAD pass. It's pure curve *structure* (knot times), so it never changes as the market moves — it's never recomputed.
- **`DF = exp(−W·x)`** is recomputed fresh at the current `x` — one `W·x` matvec + an `exp`. Cheap.
- **`∂r/∂DF`** (the per‑instrument sensitivity — the par‑rate quotient rule, the futures compounding, etc.) is recomputed analytically and scattered in. Also cheap, no AAD.
- Then we **factorize** the new `J` and form `M = J⁻¹`, which becomes the preconditioner for the rest of that tick and subsequent ticks.

So AAD has been fully retired from the streaming hot path — it runs exactly **once, ever**, to produce `W`. Every recompute after that is the closed‑form expression on the cached `W`.

Two small precisions:
- The recompute happens at the **current (not‑yet‑converged) iterate**, not at the true solution — that's fine, because `M ≈ J(x)⁻¹` there is an excellent preconditioner and the very next step lands on the answer.
- `set_anchor` also resets the reference point (`x_anchor`, `q_anchor` ← current), so the displayed drift resets to zero — that's what makes the sawtooth restart at each amber mark.

And yes — given all this, the "30 bp" is just a descriptive readout of how far a *level* move happened to travel before the step‑count trigger fired; the trigger itself is "frozen‑Newton stalled," which is the honest, direction‑aware signal.

Shall I resume the consolidation now (docs + both gates + commit)?

Key finding: `calibrate()` evaluates the **curve object** in its inner loop — `residuals<Scalar>` builds `make_calibration_curve<Scalar>` and prices off `c.discount`/`c.forward`, for both `double` and `ad::Dual`, and that's exactly the curve‑build benchmark path. ## 7a. Stage 2 — warm re-calibration to microseconds

Goal: re-calibrate after a *small* market perturbation from a solved curve in microseconds. Three
measured levers (the order matters — measure before optimising, CLAUDE.md discipline):

- **Cached-Jacobian Newton (`swaps/calibration/warm.hpp`, `WarmCalibrator`).** A warm re-cal doesn't
  need a full LM: cache `J0` (and its factorization) at the base solution and take frozen-Jacobian
  Gauss-Newton steps. **Automatic envelope detection** — if frozen steps stop converging, `J0` is
  stale (perturbation outside the reuse envelope) and it auto-refreshes. Full LM 2.8 ms → **48 µs**
  exact (matches full LM to ~1e-13).
- **First-order live-tick update = ONE matvec.** At the base `r(x0) = -dq` exactly, so the first
  Newton step is `x = x0 + M·dq` with `M = (JᵀJ)⁻¹Jᵀ` precomputed — which is the *same* operator as
  the analytic risk ladder `dx/dq`. **168 ns**, error `O(|dq|²)` (~1e-6 at 1bp). This is the
  microsecond path for real-time ticks; `recalibrate()` (48 µs, exact) is the fallback for big moves.
- **Vectorized compiled residual (`compiled_residual.hpp` on `pricing/compiled.hpp`).** The
  calibration instruments are just a portfolio valued off `DF = exp(-Wx)`; `CompiledResidual` shares
  that engine. **Honest result: only ~1.3× vs the scalar kernel** — our scalar residual was already
  fast (no virtual dispatch, telescoped, L1-resident), so the `W`-cache that gave 126× vs QuantLib's
  slow per-swap loop gives little here. It's the DRY unification, not the speed lever.

> **Measured, not assumed:** the warm-recal working set is ~9 KB (L1-resident), so cache-placement /
> memory-hierarchy tuning buys ~0. The wins are algorithmic (cached `J0`, the one-matvec update),
> not memory management.

### The accuracy-first streaming path (`swaps/calibration/streaming.hpp`, `StreamingCalibrator`)
For a **live pricer to sharp clients**, a stale price is a free option — so the default streaming mode
is `exact`: **iterate the cached `M = J⁻¹` as a frozen-Newton *preconditioner* to convergence every
tick** (`x ← x − M·(model_rates(x) − q)` until `‖dx‖∞ < 1e-9`), not a single linear extrapolation.
- The fixed point is `r = 0` **for any invertible `M`**, so every tick lands on the EXACT solution
  (round-trip `‖model_rates(x) − q‖∞ ≈ 1e-12`, machine-exact) regardless of `M`'s accuracy. `M` only
  sets the convergence *rate* `ρ = ‖I − M·J(x)‖` (measured: ~0.04 at 10 bp of drift → ~3 steps/tick).
- **The Jacobian is recomputed only on genuine staleness** — when frozen-Newton needs more than
  `max_frozen` steps — NOT on a drift envelope. That staleness envelope is ~30 bp of curve move (a
  level move; `tools/jacobian_staleness.cpp` measures `ρ` vs move size) vs the linear path's 0.35 bp,
  so ~85× fewer recomputes AND exact. The recompute reuses the cached `W` (analytic `J`, no AAD).
- **The legacy `linear` single-step path (`x = x_anchor + M·dq`, O(dq²) error, re-anchor at 0.35 bp)
  is a *smooth-market artifact*.** Under a realistic **~0.15 bp/tick** feed it re-anchors ~20% of
  ticks (drift crosses 0.35 bp every few ticks); the exact path rides one Jacobian all day. The
  "168 ns / 98% fast-path" numbers above assume an unrealistically smooth crawl — keep them for the
  *WarmCalibrator small-perturbation* use, not the live tick feed. Gate: `tests/streaming_test.cpp`
  (round-trip + exactness every tick). Demo: `tools/stream_sim.cpp` (trending day, both modes).

PRECONDITIONER to convergence every tick (x -= M*(model_rates(x)-q) until ||dx||<1e-9),

envelope: ~85x fewer recomputes AND exact. The legacy single-step path is kept behind

tick over 400 chained moves to 25bp, and zero recalcs on sub-bp moves.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# checkpoint.sh — the ONLY sanctioned path to a major checkpoint + web backup.
#   1. runs both gates (verify.sh) and refuses to proceed unless they pass
#   2. commits the working tree
#   3. tags an annotated checkpoint-NN
#   4. pushes to the web backup remote 'origin' (private GitHub repo) — only if it exists
#
# Usage: ./tools/checkpoint.sh "feat(curve): global LM calibration landing"
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
cd "${ROOT}"

MSG="${1:-}"
if [ -z "${MSG}" ]; then echo "usage: checkpoint.sh \"commit message\"" >&2; exit 2; fi

echo ">> running gates before checkpoint"
VERIFY_OUT="$(mktemp)"
if ! ./tools/verify.sh | tee "${VERIFY_OUT}"; then
  echo "!! gates failed — refusing to checkpoint. Fix correctness/perf first." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Report the ACTUAL gate status in the trailer. Never claim "perf passing" when the
# perf gate merely skipped — a commit trailer that overstates verification is worse
# than none, because later work trusts it.
gate() { grep -E "^  $1 gate:" "${VERIFY_OUT}" | awk '{print $NF}'; }
C_STATUS="$(gate correctness)"; P_STATUS="$(gate performance)"
rm -f "${VERIFY_OUT}"
TRAILER="Verified: correctness=${C_STATUS:-UNKNOWN} perf=${P_STATUS:-UNKNOWN}"

if [ "${P_STATUS}" != "PASS" ]; then
  echo ">> NOTE: perf gate is '${P_STATUS}' — this checkpoint is not perf-verified."
fi

# Next checkpoint number.
last="$(git tag --list 'checkpoint-*' | sed 's/checkpoint-//' | sort -n | tail -1)"
next=$(printf '%02d' $(( ${last:-0} + 1 )))
tag="checkpoint-${next}"

git add -A
git commit -m "${MSG}

${TRAILER}

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>" || echo "(nothing to commit)"
git tag -a "${tag}" -m "${MSG}"
echo ">> created ${tag}"

# Web backup — only if a remote is configured. Never auto-creates one.
if git remote get-url origin >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo ">> pushing ${tag} to web backup (origin)"
  git push origin main --tags
else
  echo ">> no 'origin' remote yet — skipping web backup."
  echo "   To enable: create the private GitHub repo and 'git remote add origin <url>'."
fi

message.content: Rather than move onto another currency, I'd like to introduce the idea of a curve bundle where multiple curves are calibrated simultaneously and where they can have interdependence.  For instance currently we are building a single SOFR curve where the discount and forecast curve are the same.  If I want to build a FF-OIS curve using a combiantion of FF averaging futures in the first year and then FF-SOFR basis swaps where SOFR is the discount curve then these two curves must be calbrated together

content.text:
Great direction — this is the natural "Stage 3," and the good news is our architecture already has the seam for it. Let me lay out the design, the one insight that makes it cheap, then what genuinely needs building.

## The concept, made precise

A **CurveBundle** is *N* curves sharing one **stacked parameter vector** `x = [x_S ; x_F ; …]`, calibrated by a **single joint solve**. Instruments reference curves **by role** — a *forecast* curve and a *discount* curve per leg — and the coupling falls out of which curves each instrument touches. Your FF‑OIS example maps exactly:

| curve | knots | instruments that pin it |
|---|---|---|
| **SOFR** `x_S` | FOMC front + futures/swap back (as today) | SOFR futures + SOFR swaps → self‑determined |
| **FF** `x_F` | FF‑future end dates (yr 1) + basis‑swap maturities | FF averaging futures (forecast FF) + **FF‑SOFR basis swaps** |

The basis swap is the coupler: its FF leg **forecasts off `x_F`, discounts off `x_S`**; its SOFR leg forecasts and discounts off `x_S`. So its residual depends on **both** blocks — and that's why they must calibrate together.

## The insight that makes it (mostly) free

Our LM, exact frozen‑Newton streaming, analytic Jacobian, and risk ladder are all written against an abstract *problem* — anything exposing `residuals<Scalar>(x)`, `n_knots()`, `n_residuals()`. **A bundle is just another such problem over the stacked `x`.** It internally splits `x` into per‑curve blocks, builds each curve, prices each instrument off its referenced curves, and stacks the residuals. Then:

- **`calibrate()`** drives it unchanged — one joint LM over `[x_S; x_F]`.
- **Streaming** drives it unchanged — the cached `M = J⁻¹` is just bigger; frozen‑Newton over the stack is exact every tick.
- **Risk** drives it unchanged — `dx/dq = M` now spans both curves, so a SOFR quote's delta onto the FF curve is automatic.

The Jacobian is **block‑structured**: SOFR‑only instruments have a zero FF block, FF‑only a zero SOFR block, basis swaps populate both. With per‑curve weights `DF_k = exp(-W_k x_k)`, the analytic Jacobian generalizes directly — `dr/dDF_k · (−diag(DF_k)·W_k)` scattered into curve `k`'s column block. No new solver, no AAD back on the hot path.

## What genuinely needs building

1. **Multi‑curve pricing kernel** — the one real gap. Today `ois_swap_npv(sched, curve)` assumes forecast = discount. Add a **dual‑curve** form: forecast off one curve, discount off another (plain‑data schedules already separate the two). This is the FF leg of the basis swap.
2. **`BundleProblem`** — curve specs + instruments carrying `{forecast_id, discount_id}` refs → stacked `residuals<Scalar>(x)`. Implements the problem interface so the whole solver stack picks it up.
3. **Per‑curve `W` + block Jacobian** in `CompiledResidual` for the streaming/analytic path.
4. **QuantLib extractors** for FF averaging futures and FF‑SOFR basis swaps (reuse QuantLib's instrument/convention machinery, extract plain‑data schedules once — same pattern as today).
5. **Each curve → its own `YieldTermStructure`** via the adapter we just generalized, so QuantLib prices the basis swaps off the pair (forecast FF YTS + discount SOFR YTS) — the oracle for the dual‑curve kernel.
6. **Golden + gates**: recover a known 2‑curve bundle; stationarity on the real market; dual‑curve pricing vs QuantLib to 1e‑10.

## Two decisions before I build

Everything above is joint/simultaneous. There's a lighter staged variant worth naming, and a scope choice:

## What's now working

A `BundleProblem` holds any number of curves over one stacked `x = [x_0; x_1; …]`, with instruments referencing curves by role (`Swap{curve}`, `Basis{forecast, discount}`). message.content: What conventions did you use for the PRIME and PRIME2 basis swaps

content.text:
Precise answer — and I'll flag where they're deliberately simplified, since these are synthetic framework instruments, not real Prime conventions.

## The structure I used

Every basis instrument is a **single‑currency floating‑floating swap**, both legs **SOFR‑discounted**, annual schedule, with the par spread quoted on the *new* (forecast) leg. The kernel is `basis_par_spread_annual(pay, α, fwd, bench, disc)`:

- **Spread leg** forecasts `fwd`, pays coupon + `s`.
- **Benchmark leg** forecasts `bench`.
- Each floating coupon over `[t_{i-1}, t_i]` is the **compounded index return from the forecast curve**, `DF(t_{i-1})/DF(t_i) − 1`, discounted at `DF_disc(t_i)`.
- Par spread: `s = (PV_bench − PV_spread) / Σ αᵢ·DF_disc(tᵢ)` — the spread added to the *forecast* leg to equate the two legs.

So for the chain (all `discount = SOFR`):

| curve | forecast | benchmark | reads as |
|---|---|---|---|
| PRIME (2) | PRIME | FF | pay PRIME + s vs receive FF, SOFR‑discounted |
| PRIME2 (3) | PRIME2 | PRIME | pay PRIME2 + s vs receive PRIME, SOFR‑discounted |

**Sign convention:** `s > 0` when the forecast leg's index is *below* the benchmark. That's why PRIME‑FF came out **negative** (‑326 bp: PRIME ≈ 7% is *above* FF ≈ 3.9%, so you subtract from the PRIME leg to match FF). It's a self‑consistent convention, not the colloquial "prime is 300 over."

## The key modeling choice

**PRIME and PRIME2 are each represented as their own OIS‑style forecast curve** — a discount‑factor curve whose instantaneous forward is the PRIME rate — and every floating coupon uses the *compounded* return `DF(t_{i-1})/DF(t_i)−1`, identical to how SOFR and FF are modeled. That's what makes the whole thing a clean coupled system: four curves, same accrual math, differing only in which curve each leg forecasts.

## What's simplified vs a real Prime basis

I want to be honest that these are framework instruments — the conventions are deliberately toy so the test isolates the *curve coupling*, not accrual detail:

1. **Compounded, not averaged.** Real Prime is an administered rate that accrues by **arithmetic average** (like FF averaging futures), not daily compounding. A faithful Prime leg would use a simple/averaged accrual; I used compounded `DF`‑ratio for all four curves.
2. **Single annual schedule, both legs.** Real basis swaps often mismatch leg frequencies/day‑counts and carry a payment lag; I used one annual schedule, `α = 1` (stub for < 1y).
3. **Prime as a calibrated curve at all.** In practice Prime is admin‑set (≈ SOFR/FF + a fixed spread), so you might model it as a deterministic spread rather than calibrate a curve. I calibrated it *as a genuine spread curve from basis quotes* precisely to exercise the framework's chain capability — which is the point of the test.
4. **No convexity/timing adjustments** on the floating legs.

None of that changes what the test proves — N curves, joint solve, correct chain dependency (PRIME2 depends on PRIME + SOFR, zero FF). When we wire the **real** market, the Prime leg switches to averaged accrual with real QuantLib‑extracted schedules and conventions, and only the per‑leg pricing changes — the bundle machinery stays identical.

Want me to make the synthetic Prime legs **arithmetic‑average** (closer to real Prime) before we move on, or keep the toy compounded form for the framework test and put real conventions in with the actual market wiring?

No — and that's an important gap to be honest about. The bundle work so far is **not** QuantLib‑validated. Here's the exact state:

**What the bundle tests actually do:** `bundle_test.cpp` is in the QuantLib‑*free* binary. The instruments are hand‑built annual schedules, priced with my own closed‑form kernel (`dual_curve.hpp`), and the market rates are generated **from that same kernel** (`market = model(x_true)`). So it's a **self‑referential recovery test** — calibrate inverts my own pricing.

**The critical weakness of that:** a recovery test is *blind to pricing‑formula errors*. If my `basis_par_spread_annual` had the wrong sign, a missing term, or a bad convention, I'd generate the quotes *with* that bug and recover them *with* the same bug — and the test would still pass at 1e‑15. It validates the **machinery** (stacked `x`, block Jacobian, joint solve, chain dependency) but proves nothing about whether the dual‑curve *pricing* is correct. Only an independent oracle catches that.

**The pole star is intact for everything else** — `pricing_test` and `modular_curve_test` (including the Hermite‑curve‑as‑YTS test we just added) still price our curves through QuantLib to ~1e‑16. It's specifically the **bundle / dual‑curve layer** that hasn't been put under QuantLib yet, because you (rightly) chose "framework first."

**How to close it** — and QuantLib fully supports this, since it's a genuine multi‑curve pricer:
- Wrap each bundle curve as a `YieldTermStructure` (the adapter's already generic).
- Build the basis swaps as **QuantLib instruments** with the forecast index linked to one YTS and the **discount engine linked to the SOFR YTS** — QuantLib's standard dual‑curve setup (forecast ≠ discount).
- FF is a standard overnight index; **PRIME/PRIME2 need custom `OvernightIndex` definitions** (QuantLib has no Prime index built in), forecasting off their YTS.
- Then assert our `basis_par_spread_annual` matches QuantLib's basis‑swap fair spread to 1e‑10 — the same composite‑oracle pattern as the single‑curve kernel.

That's the honest next step to bring the bundle under the pole star, and it also settles the convention question from the last message (real averaged‑Prime accrual would come in with the real QuantLib instruments).

49/49 green — the curve bundle now sits **under the QuantLib pole star**.

## Where we are

Every bundle instrument is a real `QuantLib::OvernightIndexedSwap` (`MakeOIS`) with its forecast index linked to the curve's `YieldTermStructure` and the **discount curve set to SOFR** — QuantLib's standard multi‑curve setup. The market is QuantLib's own fair rates/spreads, and:

- **Oracle**: our dual‑curve kernel reprices QuantLib's quotes to **1.25e‑16** at the true curves — machine precision, for the full SOFR → FF → PRIME → PRIME2 chain (2‑ and 4‑curve).
- **Recovery**: the single joint LM recovers all curves from those QuantLib quotes to **2.3e‑15**, 5 iterations.
- Realistic quotes fall out: SOFR 10y 4.17%, FF‑SOFR +8 bp, PRIME‑FF −321 bp, PRIME2‑PRIME −53 bp.

## What changed to get here (the honest upgrade)

The earlier synthetic bundle was self‑referential — I flagged it couldn't catch a pricing bug. So I:
- **Extended the *proven* OIS kernel to dual‑discount** (`cashflows.hpp`): the schedule already carried `float_acc_start/end` (forecast) separately from `float_pay` (discount), so `ois_par_rate(sched, fc, dc)` and `basis_par_spread(sched, fwd, bench, disc)` are a small, faithful generalization — no toy math (deleted `dual_curve.hpp`).
- **Rebuilt `BundleProblem` on real extracted OIS schedules**, so recovery and oracle share one instrument set.
- **Custom `OvernightIndex` for FF/PRIME/PRIME2** (QuantLib has no Prime index), each forecasting off its curve's YTS.

One real bug caught along the way, worth noting: `RelinkableHandle` **copies share their link**, so building the handle vector with `assign(N, …)` relinked every curve to the last one (SOFR read 7.82% off the PRIME2 curve). `resize` gives independent handles.

So — yes, to your question two messages ago: we now build all instruments in QuantLib and price through YTS, and our kernel matches to machine precision.

One thing I *dropped* in the rewrite: the explicit "block‑Jacobian / dependency‑chain" assertion (that PRIME2 has zero direct FF dependence). Recovery exercises it implicitly, but I can re‑add it as a cheap `aad_jacobian` check on the QuantLib bundle if you want it back.

This is a clean, self‑contained increment (dual kernel + real bundle + QuantLib oracle, 49/49). Want me to **re‑add the chain‑structure assertion and commit this as `checkpoint‑10`**, or keep going first (e.g., the streaming/compiled W‑path for the bundle → real‑time cross‑curve risk)?

content.text:
Not difficult at all — and the design is cleaner than "SOFR‑first‑then‑global," because the dependency structure tells you *exactly* what needs a joint solve and what doesn't.

## Detecting the dependencies is easy

Each instrument already declares its curve roles. The rule: **curve `c` (the one an instrument's forecast leg pins) depends on every *other* curve that instrument references as benchmark or discount.** Scan the instrument list → a directed graph. For the 4‑curve chain:

```
SOFR   : forecast SOFR                          → depends on {}
FF     : forecast FF,  bench SOFR,  disc SOFR    → depends on {SOFR}
PRIME  : forecast PRIME, bench FF,   disc SOFR    → depends on {SOFR, FF}
PRIME2 : forecast PRIME2, bench PRIME, disc SOFR  → depends on {SOFR, PRIME}
```

Then **condense into strongly‑connected components and topologically sort** (~60 lines, Tarjan). That gives the general, correct rule:

- **Singleton SCC** (a curve whose dependencies are all already solved) → **local LM** over just that curve's block, with the earlier curves *frozen as constants*.
- **Multi‑curve SCC** (a genuine cycle of mutual dependence) → **global LM** over just those curves.

So you don't need to guess "which need global" — the SCC decomposition decides it. Acyclic ⇒ all local; a cycle ⇒ global only within that cycle.

## Your specific question

For this 4‑curve chain it's **fully triangular (acyclic)** — so the optimum isn't "SOFR local then the other three global." It's **all four local, in topo order**: SOFR local → FF local (SOFR fixed) → PRIME local (SOFR, FF fixed) → PRIME2 local (SOFR, PRIME fixed). No global solve is needed *at all*. A global solve over {FF, PRIME, PRIME2} would be wasted work, because they're themselves a chain, not a cycle.

## The nice part: the kernel already supports it

Freezing a solved curve is free because the dual‑curve functions are templated **per curve argument**:
```cpp
basis_par_spread<Scalar>(sched, FwdCurve, BenchCurve, DiscCurve)  // three independent types
```
So a block's free curve is `CalibrationCurve<Dual>` while the frozen ones are `CalibrationCurve<double>` — the arithmetic promotes to `Dual` carrying derivatives **only w.r.t. the free block's knots**. No kernel change needed; the AAD Jacobian is automatically the small per‑block one.

## Would it be faster? Yes, and here's the estimate

The joint solve is one 28‑knot LM. Staged is 4 × 7‑knot LMs. The cost is dominated by (a) the AAD Jacobian — width shrinks 28 → 7, and each block prices only its 7 instruments, so AAD work ≈ 4×(7×7)=196 vs 28×28=784, ~4× less — and (b) the linear solve, 4×7³ vs 28³, ~16× less. So I'd expect staged ≈ **3–5× faster than the joint 2.94 ms → roughly 0.6–1 ms** for this chain.

And you're exactly right that it makes the QuantLib comparison **like‑for‑like**: staged‑local vs `IterativeBootstrap` are both sequential, curve‑by‑curve. Whether we still win there is genuinely uncertain — bootstrap's 1‑D root‑finds are cheap, but our AAD + templated kernel beats its per‑coupon object pricing. That's the measurement worth having.

## What it takes to build

Moderate — ~150–250 lines, no kernel changes:
1. Dependency graph + Tarjan SCC + topo sort over the bundle's instruments.
2. A `calibrate_staged(bundle)` driver: for each SCC in order, run an LM over that block's knots with earlier blocks frozen (a `residuals` variant that seeds only the block's curves). Singleton block ⇒ effectively a 1‑curve LM; multi ⇒ joint over the cycle.
3. Keep the joint `calibrate` as the fallback / for fully‑cyclic bundles.

Results are in — and they overturn one of my assumptions:

| 4‑curve build | time | vs our staged |
|---|---|---|
| QuantLib GlobalBootstrap | 53.4 ms | 30× |
| QuantLib **IterativeBootstrap** | 49.5 ms | **27×** |
| Ours joint LM | 2.76 ms | 1.5× |
| **Ours staged** (auto local/global) | **1.80 ms** | — |

(2‑curve: staged **0.78 ms**, 32× vs Iterative, 34× vs Global.)

Three honest takeaways:

1. **The like‑for‑like race is decisive: staged beats QuantLib's IterativeBootstrap by ~27–32×.** You were right that this is the fair comparison (both sequential, curve‑by‑curve). We win big because QuantLib's bootstrap — whichever solver — is bottlenecked on **per‑coupon overnight‑swap object pricing**, not the root‑finder.

2. **IterativeBootstrap is barely faster than GlobalBootstrap here (49.5 vs 53.4 ms, ~7%).** That surprised me — for single‑curve, iterative is much cheaper. In this dual‑discount multi‑curve setup the pricing cost dominates the solver choice, so the "iterative is way cheaper" caveat mostly evaporates. Good to know, and honest.

3. **Staging helped less than I predicted — 1.3–1.5×, not 3–5×.** My estimate over‑weighted the AAD/linear‑algebra savings. In practice the per‑iteration cost is dominated by **rebuilding the curves each residual eval** (staged still rebuilds the frozen curves as constants every eval), and staged does more *total* iterations (22 across 4 blocks vs ~5 joint). The AAD‑width and system‑size wins are real but second‑order.

The staged decomposition itself works exactly as designed — the chain auto‑splits into four singleton SCCs `{0}{1}{2}{3}`, so it's four local solves with no global step, and it recovers to 1.4e‑15 (new gate test passes).

There's a clear next optimization if you want staging to pull further ahead: **freeze the solved curves' discount factors at the cashflow times once per block** instead of rebuilding those curves on every residual eval — that removes the dominant per‑eval cost and should push staged toward the 2–3× I hoped for. But even now, the headline stands: **our staged multi‑curve build is ~30× faster than QuantLib's, on the honest sequential‑vs‑sequential comparison.**

Want me to (a) do that frozen‑DF optimization and re‑measure, and/or (b) commit the whole bundle stage — dual kernel, QuantLib oracle, staged solver, benchmarks — as `checkpoint‑10`?

**Instruments:** each curve is pinned by 7 quotes at `{0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10}y` → 7 knots per curve (so 14 total for 2‑curve, 28 for 4‑curve). All of them are OIS/basis swaps:

**The curve type is right, the structure isn't.** Each curve is `make_calibration_curve` = `MultiRegionCurve<Flat, Hermite>` — flat‑forward front + Hermite back, the same type as production. **But** I used `meeting = {0.5y}` — a *single* flat front segment — not the real **6 FOMC meeting‑date** staircase, and there are **no SOFR futures** (no 1M averaged, no 3M compounded, no Hull‑White convexity). So the front is one flat piece pinned by a 0.5y OIS, not the meeting‑date policy staircase pinned by futures.

For contrast, the production single‑SOFR reference market is **23 knots (6 meetings + 17 back)** and **29 instruments (12×1M + 8×3M futures + 9 swaps)** — much larger and structurally richer than the 7‑pillar OIS curve I benchmarked.

**What that means for the numbers.** The multi‑curve *machinery* is fully real and QuantLib‑validated to 1e‑16 (dual‑discount pricing, the chain, joint/staged solves). But the **build‑time ratios (~30×) are for a small, OIS‑only 7‑knot curve**, not the production 23‑knot SOFR with futures. On the bigger, richer curve the absolute times grow on both sides and the ratio could move — our AAD advantage tends to widen with more instruments, but QuantLib's futures helpers and the meeting‑date front change the mix, so I wouldn't quote the 30× as the production number.

I simplified deliberately to isolate the multi‑curve coupling (dual pricing + dependency chain) without also standing up FF averaging futures and four meeting‑date fronts. But you're right to flag it.

content.text:
Committed (`d80e199`, local — a follow‑up to the pushed `checkpoint-10`). Here's the production‑sized picture:

## Bundle build, 4 curves × 16‑tenor swap grid (64 knots)

| build | time | vs ours (joint) |
|---|---|---|
| QuantLib GlobalBootstrap | 808 ms | 64× |
| QuantLib **IterativeBootstrap** | 258 ms | **20×** |
| Ours joint LM | **12.7 ms** | — |
| Ours staged | 11.9 ms | 1.1× |

(2‑curve: ours ~5 ms vs QuantLib 130 ms iterative / 406 ms global.)

**Three honest takeaways:**

1. **The like‑for‑like race holds at scale: ~20–22× faster than QuantLib's IterativeBootstrap**, ~64–68× vs GlobalBootstrap. At production size the win is unambiguous, and it's the same root cause throughout — our AAD Jacobian + templated kernel vs QuantLib's per‑coupon object pricing.

2. **Iterative is now clearly cheaper than Global (258 vs 808 ms)** — at 16 tenors the sequential 1‑D bootstrap's advantage finally shows, unlike the toy 7‑pillar case where they were within 7%. Good that we're comparing against the fast one.

3. **Staging stopped helping (≈1.1× vs joint), reversing the small‑bundle result.** At 64 knots the per‑eval cost is dominated by rebuilding the curves each residual evaluation, and staged pays that plus more total iterations. So the decomposition is architecturally valuable (it's what lets *local* solves happen, and it's required for cyclic dependencies) but it is **not** a reliable speed lever — I won't oversell it.

**One caveat I'll state plainly:** this benchmark uses an **OIS‑only** grid for a clean apples‑to‑apples comparison (both sides bootstrap from OIS). The full **meeting‑date front + 1M/3M futures + basis** structure lives in the validated *test* (`BundleRealistic`, recovers to 1e‑13, matches QuantLib to 2.5e‑17) — building QuantLib rate‑helper equivalents for the FF averaging futures is the extra work a fully‑faithful *benchmark* would need, and I'd flag that as the remaining gap rather than claim the 20× is on the exact futures structure.

Want me to push this bench commit to the backup, or leave it local until the next checkpoint?

Before I touch ~15 files, one real fork to confirm — the rest is mechanical.

**"dual‑curve"** is just naming (4 spots: 2 comments, a test name, an assertion) — the functions *are* the bundle's multi‑curve kernel, so I'll rename "dual‑curve" → "multi‑curve", not remove anything.

**`TwoRegionForwardCurve`** is a `MultiRegionCurve<Flat, NaturalCubic>` wrapper. The wrinkle: the **natural‑cubic** back end is specifically what's validated against QuantLib's own interpolator (`curve_test` golden), and it's the base for `SpreadCurve`. The shipped calibration curve is `Flat+Hermite` (`make_calibration_curve`). So removing the wrapper forces a choice on the natural‑cubic:

One curve type everywhere; NaturalCubic stays only as an available region policy. Cleanest, but retires the natural-cubic-vs-QuantLib interpolation golden.

options.label: Keep natural cubic as a policy

## 7b. Stage 3 — the curve bundle (N curves calibrated together)

`BundleProblem` (`calibration/bundle_problem.hpp`) calibrates **N curves simultaneously** over one
stacked `x = [x_0; x_1; …]`. Instruments reference curves BY ROLE — a `forecast`, a `benchmark`
(for basis quotes) and a `discount` curve — so a discount curve ≠ its forecast curve. The multi-curve
pricing kernel (`pricing/cashflows.hpp`) is a faithful extension of the single-curve one: the OIS
schedule already separates `float_acc_start/end` (forecast) from `float_pay` (discount), so
`ois_par_rate(sched, fc, dc)` and `basis_par_spread(sched, fwd, bench, disc)` just thread two curves.
`fc == dc` reduces to the single-curve form. This is exactly QuantLib's multi-curve setup and is
validated against it to ~1e-16 (`tests/bundle_test.cpp`, a realistic SOFR + FF + PRIME + PRIME2 chain,
all SOFR-discounted, 73 knots / 85 instruments; joint & staged recover to ~1e-13).

- **It reuses everything.** `BundleProblem` exposes the SAME `residuals<Scalar>(x)` / `n_knots` /
  `n_residuals` interface, so `calibrate`, `aad_jacobian`, `StreamingCalibrator` and the risk ladder
  drive it UNCHANGED. The block-structured Jacobian falls straight out of AAD over the stacked
  residual — a curve-0-only instrument has an identically-zero derivative w.r.t. curve-1's knots.
- **Staged solve (`bundle_stage.hpp`).** Decompose the dependency graph (Tarjan SCC), solve each SCC
  in dependency order: a **singleton** SCC → a LOCAL LM over just that curve's block with earlier
  curves FROZEN as constants; a **cycle** → a joint LM over just its members. Frozen curves must carry
  a block-SIZED zero gradient (`xb[0]*0.0`), not an empty one, or Eigen `AutoDiffScalar` adds
  mismatched-size derivative vectors → NaN. Honest result: staging beats the joint solve on small
  bundles but ~ties it at production size (curve-rebuild-per-eval dominates); the real win is that both
  are **~20× faster than QuantLib IterativeBootstrap, ~64× vs GlobalBootstrap** (`bench/bundle_build_bench.cpp`).

+  in dependency order: a **singleton** SCC → a LOCAL LM over just that curve's block with earlier
+  curves FROZEN as constants; a **cycle** → a joint LM over just its members. Frozen curves must carry
